topic: the concept of a normal force

options.text: The support force a surface exerts perpendicular to itself, pushing back against an object resting on it
options.feedback: Correct -- when a book rests on a table, the table pushes back up on the book with a normal force.

options.text: A force that only exists in normal, everyday weather
options.feedback: "Normal" here refers to being perpendicular (at a right angle) to a surface, not to typical/usual weather.

options.text: The force of gravity pulling an object down
options.feedback: That's weight/gravity, a completely different force from the normal force.
Friction is a separate force, acting parallel to a surface, unlike the normal force, which acts perpendicular to it.

medium.text: A 10 kg box rests motionless on a flat table. If gravity pulls the box down with about 98 N of force, what is the magnitude of the normal force from the table?

options.feedback: Correct -- since the box isn't accelerating, the normal force must exactly balance gravity's downward pull.
If there were no normal force, the box would fall through the table -- there must be an equal, opposing force.
This doubles the force unnecessarily -- the normal force only needs to balance gravity exactly, not exceed it.
This is only half of what's needed to balance gravity's pull -- the box would still be accelerating downward if this were true.

hard.text: A box sits on a ramp inclined at an angle. Compared to the box's full weight, is the normal force on an inclined surface generally greater than, less than, or equal to the box's weight?

options.text: Less than the box's full weight, since only the component of weight perpendicular to the ramp's surface is balanced by the normal force
options.feedback: Correct -- on an incline, gravity's force splits into components; the normal force only counteracts the perpendicular component, which is less than the total weight.

options.text: Always exactly equal to the box's full weight, just like on a flat surface
options.feedback: This is only true on a perfectly flat, horizontal surface -- on an incline, the normal force is less than full weight due to gravity's components.

options.text: Always greater than the box's full weight
options.feedback: The normal force on an incline is actually less than the full weight, not greater, since it only balances part of gravity's effect.

options.text: Zero, regardless of the incline's angle
options.feedback: The normal force isn't zero as long as the box is resting on the surface -- it's just less than the full weight on an incline.

easy.hard: This force acts at a right angle to the surface an object rests upon, providing support.
easy.medium: This is the pushing-back force a surface exerts on an object resting on it.
easy.easy: This is the force a table pushes back up on something sitting on it.

medium.hard: Since the box isn't accelerating, the net force must be zero, meaning the normal force must exactly cancel gravity's pull.
medium.medium: Since the box isn't moving, the upward and downward forces on it must be perfectly balanced.
medium.easy: Since the box just sits there, the normal force must exactly match gravity's pull of 98 N.

hard.hard: On an incline, gravity's force vector decomposes into components parallel and perpendicular to the surface; the normal force balances only the perpendicular component, which is less than the total gravitational force.
hard.medium: On a slanted surface, only part of gravity's pull acts straight into the ramp -- the normal force only needs to balance that smaller part.
hard.easy: On a slanted surface, gravity's pull splits up, so the normal force only has to balance part of it, not all of it.
